heading: What is your space actually costing you?
intro: Ten questions about the room you work in. Answer honestly rather than aspirationally, because the point is to find the leaks, not to score well. Nothing is stored unless you ask for the audit at the end.
instruction: Pick the answer closest to what happens on a normal day, not your best day.

questions.prompt: A guest sits down. Before you touch their hair or skin, what happens?

options.text: I start. Talking through it as I go feels natural.
I usually say something first, but not every time.
I name the touch before it lands, every time, out loud.

questions.prompt: Your loudest recurring sound. Blow dryer, milk steamer, clipper, autoclave, whatever it is.

options.text: It just happens. People are used to it.
I warn people if they look nervous.
Every guest gets a warning before it starts, without me assessing them first.

questions.prompt: The lighting directly above the service chair.

options.text: Overhead, bright, and the same for everyone.
Bright, but I can turn some of it off if asked.
Dimmable or layered, and I offer the option before anyone has to ask.

questions.prompt: A guest who does not want to talk for the whole appointment.

options.text: Would be awkward. I would probably keep the conversation going.
Fine, but they would have to tell me, and most people do not.
Is a bookable option with a name, offered at intake.

questions.prompt: Your intake or booking form asks about sensory needs.

options.text: No. Allergies and contact details only.
There is a free-text notes box people could use.
Yes, with specific questions, and the answers reach whoever is doing the service.

questions.prompt: Scent in the space. Product, diffusers, candles, cleaning chemicals.

options.text: There is a signature scent, and it is part of the brand.
Nothing deliberate, but the products smell like products.
Actively managed, ventilated, and a low-scent appointment is possible.

questions.prompt: Moving the chair, tilting someone back, adjusting a headrest.

options.text: I do it. It is part of the service.
I tell them as I am moving it.
I say what is about to happen, then pause, then move.
Open, busy, music on, facing the room.
Quiet enough most of the time.
There is a low-stimulation option, or guests can wait outside and be texted.

questions.prompt: A guest goes quiet, still and agreeable halfway through a service.

options.text: Good sign. They have relaxed.
I might notice, but I would not necessarily do anything.
I recognise it as a stress response and I have a specific thing I do next.

questions.prompt: Someone needs to stop the service partway through.

options.text: Has not really come up. It would be handled in the moment.
I would manage it, but I would be improvising.
There is a written protocol, everyone on the floor knows it, and nobody apologises.

bands.label: Leaking
bands.headline: Your space is losing people quietly.
bands.body: Nothing here means you are doing a bad job. It means the room is running on defaults that were designed for a nervous system that is not under load, and the guests it does not suit are leaving without telling you why. That is the expensive kind of loss, because it never shows up as a complaint. The fastest change is the cheapest one: warning before touch and before noise. It costs nothing and it moves more than anything else on this list.
bands.next: Start with the free audit. It takes an hour and it will name the three specific things costing you the most.

bands.label: Patching
bands.headline: You are doing this by instinct, and instinct does not scale.
bands.body: You are already adapting, and the guests who benefit have probably noticed. The gap is that it depends on you reading the room correctly on the day, which means it fails when you are tired, when you are busy, and completely when someone else covers your chair. Good instinct without a written protocol is a person, not a standard. The work from here is turning what you already do into something repeatable that does not need you to be at your best.
bands.next: The audit will show you which of your adaptations are reliable and which only happen when you remember.

bands.label: Standard-Ready
bands.headline: You are most of the way there and you are not getting credit for it.
bands.body: You are already running close to the standard, which means the remaining work is smaller than you think and the bigger gap is visibility. Guests who need this cannot tell from the outside that your space is different from every other space that has hurt them before, so they never walk in. What you are missing is the written protocol, the language that says it out loud on your booking page, and something verifiable that tells a stranger this room is safe before they risk it.
bands.next: The audit will find your remaining gaps in an hour. Certification is what makes the rest of it legible to the people looking for you.

captureHeading: Want the twelve-point audit that goes with this?
captureBody: The Sensory Leak Audit walks you through your own floor and names what is costing you. It arrives straight away, along with the client-facing expectations sheet you can post on your booking page.
captureFineprint: One email with the download, then roughly one a week. Leave whenever you want.
